title: UPI debit landed. The credit never did.
explain:
A UPI payment is made for Rs 45,000.
The sender account is debited.
The receiver is never credited, and the credit acknowledgement timed out somewhere between the two banks.

Here's how that happens:

→ Local debit commits
→ Credit acknowledgement never arrives
→ Retry meets duplicate suppression
→ Message parks in an internal queue

The assumption was:
"A debit means the credit followed."

A UPI debit committed locally while the credit acknowledgement timed out, a partial commit across two systems: the sender account debited, the receiver never credited. A retry hit duplicate-suppression logic and the message parked in a queue, leaving one system committed and the other uncertain. The mitigations are globally unique transaction references, idempotent processing at each bank, compensating transactions such as auto-reversal, and settlement-level balancing at the end of the cycle.

One system committed, the other uncertain. That is a partial commit.

BA Takeaway

Design for the partial commit. Globally unique references, idempotent processing at each bank, auto-reversal as the compensating transaction, and settlement-level balancing at the end of the cycle to catch what the real-time flow missed.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Globally unique transaction reference
→ Idempotent processing at each bank
→ Auto-reversal
→ Settlement-level balancing

The real requirement isn't "Was the sender debited?"

It's "What evidence proves the credit landed, or the debit was reversed?"

Have you ever been debited on UPI while the person you paid received nothing?
takeaway: The mitigations are globally unique transaction references, idempotent processing at each bank, compensating transactions such as auto-reversal, and settlement-level balancing at the end of the cycle.

title: AC06 became MS03, and nobody could say why
explain:
A return code mapping changes: AC06 for a blocked account becomes MS03, reason not specified.
It looks like a one-line change.
Then the receiving bank asks why, the compliance team asks who approved it, and the payment engine cannot explain which blocked accounts produce AC06 at all.

Here's how that happens:

→ Core banking knows the account is blocked
→ Business interpretation decides the code
→ Country rule applied
→ Engine sends the agreed code
→ Nobody can say why AC06 became MS03

The assumption was:
"Mapping a return code is a one-line change."

Mapping AC06 for a blocked account to MS03, reason not specified, looks like a one-line change until the BA asks how core banking communicates the condition, what the payment engine actually understands, and which conditions should produce AC06 at all. Core banking may know the account is blocked for a KYC restriction, a debit block, dormancy, or another restriction, while the engine only understands that the account is blocked, and national data-protection requirements may forbid passing the specific reason downstream. The real gap is found by comparing what the ecosystem understands today with what the requirement expects, then tracing the chain from core banking through business interpretation, country rule, and mapping to the return code, and deciding which system changes and who agrees the mapping.

The gap usually sits between systems, not inside one.

BA Takeaway

Trace the chain from core banking through business interpretation, country rule and mapping to the return code. Compare what the ecosystem understands today with what the requirement expects, then decide which system changes and who agrees the mapping.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Core banking condition
→ Business interpretation
→ Country rule and data protection
→ Engine mapping
→ Agreed owner of the mapping

The real requirement isn't "What code do we send?"

It's "What evidence proves each system understands the condition, and who agreed the mapping?"

Have you ever changed a return code and found nobody could explain which accounts it applied to?
takeaway: The real gap is found by comparing what the ecosystem understands today with what the requirement expects, then tracing the chain and deciding which system changes and who agrees the mapping.

title: EUR 3,000 collection late because one of three calendars was closed
explain:
A EUR 3,000 direct debit is due on a Monday.
The creditor's bank is open, the debtor's bank is open.
The collection still does not complete that day.

Here's how that happens:

→ Creditor PSP open on the due date
→ Debtor PSP open on the due date
→ Clearing and settlement mechanism closed for a holiday
→ The collection waits until the mechanism reopens

The assumption was:
"If our bank is open, the collection will complete."

Why?

A direct debit collection depends on three calendars at once: the creditor PSP, the debtor PSP, and the clearing and settlement mechanism. If any one of them is closed on the due date, the collection cannot complete that day, even when the other two are open.

Two open calendars ≠ Three.

Planning on a single calendar, such as only the creditor's own business calendar, is what produces late debits.

BA Takeaway

Plan every collection against all three calendars.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Creditor PSP calendar
→ Debtor PSP calendar
→ Clearing and settlement mechanism calendar
→ Due date actually achievable

The real requirement isn't "Is our bank open on the due date?"

It's "What evidence proves all three calendars were open on the due date?"

Have you seen a collection go late because a third calendar nobody checked was closed?
takeaway: Planning on a single calendar, such as only the creditor's own business calendar, is what produces late debits.

explain:
A customer sent USD 25,000 overseas.
A domestic instant payment the same morning arrived in seconds.
The cross-border payment took two days.

Here is what happened:

→ pacs.008 raised for USD 25,000
→ Intermediary bank receives it after its cut-off
→ Currency conversion queued for the next window
→ Compliance and sanctions screening holds it
→ Settlement waits for the next system operating hours

The requirement said:
"Each leg is fast, so the whole payment will be fast."

So the customer was promised same-day delivery, and the promise broke at the first slow hop.

Why?

A domestic instant payment moves inside one system under one set of rules. A cross-border payment passes through several payment service providers, currency conversions, compliance checks and settlement systems. Each hop adds time, and the hops depend on each other's operating hours. A fast leg cannot rescue a chain that waits overnight.

A chain is only as fast as its slowest hop.

BA Takeaway

Each hop has its own clock, so keep them separate:

→ Intermediary cut-off and operating hours
→ Currency conversion window
→ Compliance and sanctions screening
→ Final settlement system hours

The real requirement is not "How fast is each leg?"

It is "What evidence proves the full chain can complete inside the promised time?"

Have you ever promised a fast cross-border payment that a single slow hop delayed by a day?
takeaway: A chain is only as fast as its slowest hop.

title: USD 10,000 in a French bank account, sitting in New York
explain:
A customer opens a USD 10,000 account with a bank in France.
The customer checks the balance in Paris and sees USD 10,000.
The actual dollars sit with the bank's correspondent in the USA.

Here's how that happens:

→ Customer opens a USD account with the French bank
→ The French bank records the account in its own books
→ The actual USD rests with its correspondent in the USA
→ The customer is credited only when the correspondent advises with an MT103

The assumption was:
"My dollars are in the bank where I opened the account."

Why?

When a customer opens a USD account with a bank in France, the bank records the account in its own books while the actual USD rests with its correspondent in the USA. Funding comes from the customer buying USD or receiving it from someone, and the sending bank locates the French bank's US correspondent and routes the funds there. The correspondent then advises the French bank with an MT103, and only on that advice is the customer's account credited.

A record in Paris ≠ Dollars in Paris.

BA Takeaway

Credit the customer only on the correspondent's advice, never on the local record alone.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Customer account recorded in the French bank's books
→ Actual USD held by the US correspondent
→ Funding: customer buys USD or receives it
→ MT103 advice from the correspondent, triggering the credit

The real requirement isn't "Did we record the account?"

It's "What evidence proves the correspondent holds the funds before we credit the customer?"

Have you seen a customer told their foreign currency was in the branch, when it sat overseas?
takeaway: The correspondent then advises the French bank with an MT103, and only on that advice is the customer's account credited.

title: USD 1 million nostro opened, and the first payment bounced on zero
explain:
A bank opens a new USD nostro and promises a USD 1 million payment from it the same day.
The payment bounces.
The account opened at zero, and nobody had funded it.

Here's how that happens:

→ Bank asks a US bank to open the nostro account
→ The account opens empty, at zero
→ The team promises a USD 1 million payment from it
→ The FX deal to fund it was never placed

The assumption was:
"A new nostro opens with money in it."

Why?

Currency never leaves its home country, so a bank funds a new nostro by buying the foreign currency on the FX market and naming the nostro as the account to receive it. Where no banking relationship exists yet, the bank first asks a bank in that currency's country to open the account, which starts at zero, and only then does the FX deal. Where the bank already holds the currency in an account elsewhere, it simply instructs that bank to move the funds across, with no FX deal needed.

An open account ≠ A funded account.

BA Takeaway

Fund the nostro before promising any payment from it, by FX deal or by moving funds already held.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Account opened, starting at zero
→ FX deal buying the currency, naming the nostro
→ Funds already held elsewhere, moved across
→ Payment promised only after funding lands

The real requirement isn't "Did we open the nostro?"

It's "What evidence proves the nostro was funded before the first payment was promised?"

Have you seen a payment bounce from an account that had only just been opened?
takeaway: Where the bank already holds the currency in an account elsewhere, it simply instructs that bank to move the funds across, with no FX deal needed.

title: EUR 5,000 to another country, no link to send it on
explain:
A bank wants to send EUR 5,000 instantly to a country its system has never paid.
It has no link to that country's instant system.
Building one link for every country would take years.
So the payment waits.

Here is how that happens:

→ Domestic instant system pays in seconds at home
→ No one-to-one link to the other country's system
→ Every pair of countries needs its own connection
→ Cross-border instant payment cannot start

The assumption was:
"Each country must connect to every other country."

Project Nexus takes the other path: link domestic instant payment systems across countries so a system joins Nexus a single time and through that link can pay any other country on the network.

Why?

Each national system stays independent, keeping its own rules and running its own business, while Nexus serves as the central hub and global connector. Connection is not interaction: one connection to the hub replaces a web of bilateral links.

Connect once, reach many countries.

Why does a payment that is instant at home wait days abroad?

BA Takeaway

Judge a cross-border design by connections, not by countries, and keep each system independent behind the hub.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Domestic system, its own rules, its own business
→ Nexus connection, one link to the hub
→ Reach, every other country on the network through that link

Show the hub connection and the countries it reaches on one map, not a list of bilateral links.

The real requirement is not "How many countries are we linked to?"

It is "What evidence proves one connection reaches them all?"

Have you waited on a cross-border payment that was instant at home?
takeaway: Connect once, reach many countries. A central platform replaces a web of bilateral links.

title: USD 1,000 sent abroad, USD 60 gone in cost, three days gone in time
explain:
A customer sends USD 1,000 to family abroad.
USD 60 disappears in cost.
Three days pass before it arrives.
The same amount moves in a second at home.

Here is how that happens:

→ Domestic payment, one second, low cost
→ Cross-border payment, three days, about 6 percent cost
→ Outdated cross-border system carries most of the blame
→ Instant systems already run in many countries, but the global gap stays

The assumption was:
"The money itself is slow and expensive to move."

It is the system, not the money. A payment that takes a second domestically can take three days across borders, and the outdated cross-border system carries most of the blame.

Why?

Instant payment systems have already changed this in many countries, including India with UPI, Europe with SEPA Instant, Singapore, Brazil, the United States, the United Kingdom and Thailand, yet a global money transfer is still said to cost about 6 percent of the transaction value against a target of 3 percent. Reaching people in remote areas who do not use smartphones needs processing systems, not just mobile apps.

Slow and costly is a system problem, not a money problem.

Why does USD 1,000 cost USD 60 and three days to cross a border?

BA Takeaway

Fix the system behind the payment, and design for people without smartphones as well as people with them.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Speed, seconds at home, days abroad
→ Cost, about 6 percent against a 3 percent target
→ Reach, processing systems for remote areas, not just apps

Show the cost and the arrival time before the customer confirms, and name the system behind each leg.

The real requirement is not "How fast is the payment?"

It is "What evidence proves the cost and the arrival time the customer was promised?"

Have you paid 6 percent to send money that moves in a second at home?
takeaway: Reaching people in remote areas needs processing systems, not just mobile apps.

title: EUR 20,000 instant in Europe, stuck for hours outside it
explain:
A customer sends EUR 20,000 instantly inside Europe.
It arrives in seconds.
The same customer sends EUR 20,000 just outside Europe.
It takes hours, and no one can say why.
The rail was instant. The payment was not.

Here is how that happens:

→ SCT Inst delivers instant payments across Europe
→ OCT Inst extends instant beyond Europe
→ Switches and interoperability link the systems
→ Liquidity, FX pricing, compliance and settlement still lag behind

The assumption was:
"Link the instant systems and the payment becomes instant."

Switches and interoperability do not solve everything. Liquidity, visible FX pricing and the correspondent bank role all still count, compliance has to keep up, UETR traceability helps resolve cases on time, and clearing and settlement still occur between systems.

Why?

Cross-border payments become truly instant only when rules are clear, systems are aligned, and technology works with people, so the experience of the payment matters as much as the speed. One fast leg cannot carry a chain whose other pieces run on slower clocks.

One instant leg does not make an instant payment.

Why does the payment stall for hours after the instant leg finishes in seconds?

BA Takeaway

Make every piece instant, or say plainly which piece is not.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Instant rails, SCT Inst and OCT Inst
→ Liquidity and FX transparency, priced and funded upfront
→ Compliance at instant speed, with UETR traceability
→ Clearing and settlement between systems

Show the speed of every step, not just the fastest one, and flag the slowest step to the customer.

The real requirement is not "Is the rail instant?"

It is "What evidence proves every step of this payment is fast?"

Have you watched an instant payment stall on its slowest leg?
takeaway: Cross-border payments become truly instant only when rules are clear, systems are aligned, and technology works with people.

title: EUR 25,000 instant payment, three steps fast, one step slow, promise broken
explain:
A bank promises EUR 25,000 instant payments.
The channel is fast. The engine is fast. Clearing is fast.
Settlement is slow.
The customer promise breaks, even though three steps are instant.

Here is how that happens:

→ Customer channel, fast
→ Payment engine, fast
→ Clearing, fast
→ Settlement, slow, the bottleneck
→ Customer waits, promise broken

The assumption was:
"The rail is instant, so the payment is instant."

For an instant payment to feel instant end to end, every step must be fast: the customer channel, the payment engine, clearing and settlement.

Why?

If any one step is slow, the customer promise breaks even when the other steps are instant. The work is to find which step is the bottleneck and optimise it, rather than assuming the rail alone makes the payment instant.

One slow step breaks an instant promise.

Why does an instant rail still deliver a slow payment?

BA Takeaway

Find the bottleneck step and fix it, and never sell the rail speed as the payment speed.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Customer channel, must be fast
→ Payment engine, must be fast
→ Clearing, must be fast
→ Settlement, must be fast
→ Bottleneck, the slowest step, named and fixed

Measure the time of every step, and report the slowest as the payment speed.

The real requirement is not "Is the rail instant?"

It is "What evidence proves every step is fast, including the slowest one?"

Have you promised instant and delivered it everywhere except one step?
takeaway: The work is to find which step is the bottleneck and optimise it, rather than assuming the rail alone makes the payment instant.

title: EUR 80,000 instant payment, FX quote expires while screening runs
explain:
A bank sends EUR 80,000 instantly to a non-euro account.
The FX quote is locked at 09:00.
Screening runs long.
At 09:04 the quote has expired, and the payment cannot settle at the promised rate.

Here is how that happens:

→ Bank relies on an FX provider, no liquidity in every currency
→ Provider sources quotes, locks rates, executes conversion
→ Screening runs while the quote clock ticks
→ Quote expires, or the provider has no currency when needed

The assumption was:
"The FX provider will be there when the payment needs it."

A bank that does not hold liquidity in every currency relies on an FX provider to source quotes, lock rates, execute the conversion and supply the settlement currency.

Why?

The arrangement works on quiet days, but a quote can expire while screening runs, or the provider may not have the currency when it is needed. The FX provider is a dependency in the payment chain, and its failure modes must be designed for, because a chain is only as reliable as its weakest link.

The provider is a link in the chain, not a guarantee.

Why does an instant payment fail on a quote that was good minutes ago?

BA Takeaway

Design for the quote expiring and the currency running out, and hold the payment until the FX leg is proved.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Quote, sourced and locked, with its expiry shown
→ Screening, timed against the quote clock
→ Conversion, executed only inside the quote validity
→ Settlement currency, supplied and confirmed

Show the quote expiry beside the screening time, and re-quote before executing if the clock ran out.

The real requirement is not "Was a quote locked?"

It is "What evidence proves the quote was still valid when the conversion executed?"

Have you watched a quote expire mid-payment?
takeaway: The FX provider is a dependency in the payment chain, and its failure modes must be designed for.

title: USD 100,000 instant dollars promised, no dollars to settle with on Monday morning
explain:
A bank promises instant dollar payments.
On Monday morning a customer sends USD 100,000.
The rate is competitive. The system is ready.
There are not enough dollars to settle with.

Here is how that happens:

→ Bank offers instant dollar payments at a good rate
→ Customer sends USD 100,000 on Monday morning
→ Settlement currency not held in enough volume
→ Payment fails, not on price, on liquidity

The assumption was:
"A good rate means the payment can settle."

Having a competitive exchange rate is not the same as having the settlement currency available at the moment it is needed.

Why?

A bank can offer instant dollar payments and still fail on some mornings because it does not hold enough dollars to settle. The constraint is liquidity, not conversion, and it must be managed by treasury, not just by the payment engine.

Rate is not liquidity.

Why does a payment with a great rate fail on a Monday morning?

BA Takeaway

Manage settlement liquidity with treasury, and never promise instant settlement the nostro cannot fund.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Competitive rate, what the customer is offered
→ Currency availability, what treasury holds for settlement
→ Instant promise, only where liquidity is proved
→ Treasury management, funding the nostro before the morning peak

Show the nostro balance beside the instant promise, and pause the promise when liquidity is short.

The real requirement is not "Is the rate competitive?"

It is "What evidence proves the settlement currency is held for this payment?"

Have you seen a good rate fail for want of the currency itself?
takeaway: The constraint is liquidity, not conversion, and it must be managed by treasury, not just by the payment engine.

title: EUR 45,000 across two instant systems, timeout, customer taps send again
explain:
A customer sends EUR 45,000 across two fast payment systems.
The screen times out.
The customer taps send again.
Now the bank has two instructions and one debit, and nobody knows if the money moved.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment crosses two fast payment systems joined by an orchestration layer
→ Timeout occurs, outcome uncertain
→ Money may have moved, or it may not have
→ Customer taps send again, two instructions, one debit

The assumption was:
"A timeout means it failed, so sending again is safe."

In a corridor where a payment crosses two fast payment systems joined by an orchestration layer, a timeout leaves the outcome uncertain: the money may have moved, or it may not have.

Why?

If the customer taps send again, the bank can end up with two instructions and one debit. The safe handling is to establish the true state, never retry blindly, and use an inter-PSP investigation to resolve the uncertainty.

Timeout is not failure. It is unknown.

Why does a helpful retry create a second instruction?

BA Takeaway

Never retry blind. Establish the true state first, then act on it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Timeout, outcome unknown, not failed
→ True state, established before any retry
→ Retry, only after the state is known
→ Inter-PSP investigation, resolving the uncertainty

Block the send button after a timeout until the true state is shown, and open the investigation at once.

The real requirement is not "Did the customer retry?"

It is "What evidence proves the true state was known before any retry?"

Have you seen a retry double an instruction after a timeout?
takeaway: The safe handling is to establish the true state, never retry blindly, and use an inter-PSP investigation to resolve the uncertainty.

title: One extra hour at the branch, and the RTGS payment bounced
explain:
A branch cut-off for RTGS is extended by one hour.

It sounds small. It is not.

A Rs. 50 lakh payment accepted inside the new hour is rejected downstream, because the clearing window never moved.

Here is how it happens:

→ Branch cut-off extended by one hour
→ Payment accepted inside the new hour
→ Settlement windows stay fixed
→ Core banking hours, batch jobs, standing instructions and reconciliation still read the old clock
→ Payment accepted past the clearing window is rejected downstream

The assumption was:
"Moving the cut-off is a parameter change."

Why?

A cut-off is a contract between the bank, the clearing system and every downstream batch. Moving it means re-validating everything that depends on it.

A cut-off is a contract, not a clock setting.

BA Takeaway

Treat a cut-off change as a full regression exercise, not a parameter tweak. Every dependent system must be re-validated before the new time goes live.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Branch cut-off
→ Clearing window
→ Downstream batches and reconciliation

The real requirement is not "What time is the new cut-off?"

It is "What evidence proves every dependent system reads the new cut-off?"

Have you seen a small timing change break a payment downstream?
takeaway: A cut-off is a contract, not a clock setting. Moving it means re-validating everything that depends on it.

title: The German Direct Debit flow met the Dutch customer, and failed
explain:
A Direct Debit process defined for Germany works well there.

The bank reuses it for the Netherlands.

A customer moves to a new Dutch bank, the debit for the closed account is rejected, and a EUR 5,000 monthly payment bounces. It should have been redirected.

Here is how it happens:

→ German Direct Debit process is reused for the Netherlands
→ Customer moves to a new Dutch bank
→ Debit arrives for the closed account
→ Local Overstapservice rule requires redirecting, not rejecting
→ Debit is rejected, and the payment fails

The assumption was:
"Reuse the process that worked in Germany."

Why?

The Netherlands has its own local specification, the Overstapservice, a bank-switching service that lets Direct Debits continue after a customer moves to a new Dutch bank. Reuse looks efficient, yet efficiency is not the test.

Reuse is a delivery choice, not a business decision.

BA Takeaway

Before agreeing to reuse, check whether the requirement is a common scheme rule or a local specification, and whether the new country adds requirements the existing logic never had to meet.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Common scheme rule
→ Local specification
→ New country requirements

The real requirement is not "Can we reuse this?"

It is "What evidence proves the reused logic meets the local rule?"

Have you seen a reused process fail because the new country had a rule the old one never needed?
takeaway: Reuse is a delivery choice, not a business decision. Check the local rule first.

title: USD 50,000 to a bank that is not on SWIFT
explain:
USD 50,000 had to reach a bank that is not a SWIFT member.
The MT103 could not be sent to it directly.
The payment sat for a day while the team argued whether it could be sent at all.

Here's how that happens:

→ Beneficiary bank is not a SWIFT member
→ MT103 cannot be sent to it directly
→ Member bank forwards the instruction as intermediary
→ Payment follows the usual serial or cover logic

The assumption was:
"No SWIFT membership means no payment."
Non-membership does not stop the payment. It adds a step to the chain.

Why?

The payment must reach the beneficiary bank through a bank that is a member and can forward the instruction. The forwarding bank becomes an intermediary in the chain, and the payment follows the same serial or cover logic as any other payment with an intermediary.

Non-membership does not stop the payment. It adds a step to the chain.

What proves the payment can reach a bank outside SWIFT?

BA Takeaway

Route the payment through a member bank that can forward it. Name the forwarding bank as the intermediary, and apply the same serial or cover logic as any other payment with an intermediary.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Beneficiary bank
→ Forwarding member bank
→ Route chosen
→ Payment delivered

The real requirement isn't "Can we pay a bank that is not on SWIFT?"

It's "What evidence proves the payment can reach a bank outside SWIFT?"

Have you ever had to route a payment through a forwarding bank?
takeaway: Non-membership does not stop the payment. It adds a step to the chain.

title: A small bank sent EUR 500,000 abroad. It owned no correspondent anywhere.
explain:
A small bank needs to send EUR 500,000 to a supplier overseas.
It holds no correspondent account in that currency.
The payment still goes through, and the customer never asks how.

Here is how that happens:

→ Small bank takes a EUR 500,000 payment
→ No correspondent in the payment currency
→ Large domestic bank intermediates the payment
→ Funds settle with the correspondent in the currency country

The requirement said:
"A bank must hold its own correspondent to send money abroad."

Why?

Building and maintaining a correspondent network is costly and slow, so a small bank often opens a foreign currency account with a large bank in its own country that already holds a correspondent in the currency's country. That large bank then acts as intermediary for the small bank's cross-border payments, while the real funds still end up held in the currency's country.

No correspondent of your own does not mean no route abroad.

BA Takeaway

Map the real chain on every corridor, and know which bank in the chain actually holds the funds.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Small bank account
→ Intermediary bank
→ Correspondent in the currency country

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves which bank in the chain holds the funds?"

Have you traced a payment through a bank that was only ever an intermediary?
takeaway: No correspondent of your own does not mean no route abroad.

title: Treasury bought EUR 5 million of FX. The nostro was still empty.
explain:
Treasury buys EUR 5 million to fund the day's payments.
The mirror account shows the credit.
The payments still fail, because the real nostro was never checked.

Here is how that happens:

→ Treasury buys FX to fund the day
→ Funds land in the correspondent account
→ Mirror reflects the credit
→ Real nostro balance never verified

The requirement said:
"If the mirror shows the funds, the nostro has them."

Why?

A treasury team moves no money itself. It watches balances on the correspondent accounts and buys or sells foreign exchange to hold enough funds for the day's payments. When it buys currency in the FX market, the funds land in the correspondent bank account in the foreign country, and the mirror account simply reflects that credit. The mirror does nothing on its own. It only records what happened on the real account.

Treasury funds the nostro. The mirror only records it.

BA Takeaway

Fund against the real nostro balance, confirmed by advice, never against the mirror alone.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Treasury FX trades
→ Real nostro balance
→ Mirror reflection

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves the funds actually landed in the correspondent account?"

takeaway: Treasury funds the nostro. The mirror only records it.

title: EUR 400,000 crossed two countries. The money never left the country it started in.
explain:
A EUR 400,000 payment crosses borders between two banks.
The SWIFT message travels internationally.
The money itself settles locally, and the customer is charged the international price anyway.

Here is how that happens:

→ Cover leg between two correspondents
→ Both correspondents sit in the same country
→ Local clearing settles the leg
→ Customer charged as if funds crossed borders

The requirement said:
"Cover funds always travel over SWIFT."

Why?

In a cross-border payment the cover leg moves funds between the sender's correspondent and the receiver's correspondent, and where both correspondents sit in the same country a local clearing system can settle that leg. The payment message still travels over SWIFT, but the money itself moves locally. The local route costs less than moving the funds over the SWIFT network.

Same country, same clearing. The message travels, the money stays local.

BA Takeaway

Check where both correspondents sit before choosing the cover route, and price the payment on the route the money actually takes.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Cover leg
→ Correspondent locations
→ Settlement route

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves where the cover funds actually settled?"

Have you paid international prices for money that settled locally?
takeaway: Same country, same clearing. The message travels, the money stays local.

title: A EUR 150,000 payment to Germany went by MT202 COV. SEPA would have cost less.
explain:
A bank outside Europe instructs its French correspondent to pay EUR 150,000 to a German customer.
The payment goes out as an MT202 COV.
It arrives late and expensive, when SEPA would have done it faster and cheaper.

Here is how that happens:

→ Bank outside Europe instructs its French correspondent
→ EUR 150,000 to a German bank customer
→ MT202 COV sent over SWIFT
→ SEPA route never considered

The requirement said:
"A euro payment to Europe always needs an MT202 COV."

Why?

When a bank outside Europe instructs its correspondent in France to pay a customer of a German bank in euros, it need not use an MT202 COV. The correspondent can pay through SEPA or another local system instead, and in practice that local route is the one used most often. It also costs less than sending the funds over the SWIFT network.

A euro leg in Europe belongs on SEPA, not on an MT202 COV.

BA Takeaway

Route the euro leg through the local system first, and use the SWIFT cover only when the local route cannot serve it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Euro leg
→ SEPA route
→ MT202 COV route

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves the local route could not serve this payment?"

takeaway: A euro leg in Europe belongs on SEPA, not on an MT202 COV.

title: USD 20,000 in cash, handed over in Paris. The dollars were in New York.
explain:
A customer with a USD account in France asks for USD 20,000 in cash.
The real dollars sit with the bank's correspondent in the USA.
The branch hands over the cash anyway, and the account is debited the same amount.

Here is how that happens:

→ Customer asks for USD 20,000 cash
→ Real dollars sit with the US correspondent
→ Branch pays from its cash stock
→ Same amount debited from the USD account

The requirement said:
"Foreign cash can only be paid where the currency sits."

Why?

A customer holding a USD account with a bank in France can ask for the funds in physical USD cash, even though the real dollars sit with the bank's correspondent in the USA. The bank keeps an estimated stock of USD cash on hand, sized on customer demand, and sources it from customers selling USD for euros or from another bank. It hands over the cash and debits the same amount from the customer's USD account.

Cash on hand is not the nostro. The debit is what balances it.

BA Takeaway

Keep the cash stock and the nostro apart in every control, and reconcile the cash paid against the account debited the same day.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Cash stock on hand
→ USD account debit
→ Correspondent nostro

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves the cash paid matches the account debited?"

takeaway: Cash on hand is not the nostro. The debit is what balances it.

title: A EUR 20,000 cross-border payment arrived in seconds. The customer still could not see what it cost.
explain:
A EUR 20,000 cross-border payment arrives in seconds.
The customer cannot see the FX cost, cannot trace the payment, and the remittance data is too thin for the checks.
Speed was delivered, and almost nothing else was.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 20,000 instant cross-border payment sent
→ FX cost hidden from the customer
→ Payment cannot be traced
→ Remittance data too thin for AML checks

The requirement said:
"Instant cross-border payments are only about speed."

Why?

Instant cross-border payments are not only about speed, because several pieces must work together for the whole journey to be efficient. Clearing, processing and settlement must become more efficient, FX conversion must be transparent to the customer, and payment status must be traceable, while richer remittance information supports AML and fraud checks, and common messaging standards and APIs make systems interoperable. When these pieces combine, transaction time and end-user costs fall, which is the real transformation.

Instant is only one piece. Speed without the rest is not a transformation.

BA Takeaway

Build the whole journey together: efficient settlement, transparent FX, traceability, rich remittance data and common standards.

Keep these controls separate:

→ FX transparency
→ Payment traceability
→ Remittance data
→ Common standards

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves the customer could see the cost and trace this payment?"

Have you shipped speed and called the journey done?
takeaway: Instant is only one piece. Speed without the rest is not a transformation.

title: Two instant rails were connected by API. A EUR 30,000 payment still could not cross.
explain:
Two payment systems are connected with an API.
A EUR 30,000 payment is sent across the bridge.
It fails, because messaging, rules, clearing, settlement and compliance never lined up.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 30,000 payment sent across the bridge
→ Systems connected by API
→ Rules and settlement never aligned
→ Payment cannot cross

The requirement said:
"Connecting two systems makes them interoperable."

Why?

Interoperability goes beyond connecting two systems with an API, because messaging, processing rules, clearing, settlement, compliance and day-to-day operations must also line up. A payment bridge joins two payment ecosystems in business and technical terms, where each side may run its own instant rail, currency and rules, and the bridge works as shared standards, scheme rules and cooperation between systems dictate. ISO 20022 supplies the common language, UETR supplies traceability, OCT Inst supplies rules for the Euro leg, and together they move interoperable instant payments across borders closer.

Interoperability demands more than connectivity.

BA Takeaway

Align messaging, rules, clearing, settlement, compliance and operations on every bridge, not just the connection.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Common messaging
→ Shared rules
→ Settlement alignment
→ Compliance alignment

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves the rules and settlement line up, not just the connection?"

takeaway: Interoperability demands more than connectivity.

title: The engine was open, but the USD 100,000 payment had nowhere to go
explain:
A customer sent a USD 100,000 international payment on a day the USA was open and France was closed.

The payment engine was open, so the payment was accepted.

But the French bank holding the receiving account was closed, and the credit never appeared in the customer's intraday reporting.

Here's how it happened:

→ Payment engine open, payment accepted
→ Core banking closed at the receiving bank, no account booking
→ Compliance controls unavailable
→ Nostro funding feed down
→ Intraday reporting shows nothing, the customer acts on an incomplete cash position

The requirement said:
"Process payments when the engine is open."

Why?

The engine is only one link in the chain. A payment also needs core banking, compliance, customer reporting and the nostro funding feed. Asking whether the engine is open is the wrong question.

An open engine does not mean a ready payment journey.

BA Takeaway

A holiday calendar is an end-to-end operating decision, not an engine setting. Internal and regulatory reporting and nostro reconciliation may wait under agreed controls, but the BA must not decide that alone.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Core banking and account booking
→ Compliance controls
→ Customer reporting and nostro funding
→ Reporting and reconciliation catch-up

The real requirement isn't "Is the engine open?"

It's "What evidence proves every link in the journey is ready?"

Have you seen a payment accepted on a day the rest of the journey was closed?

title: Two instant payment systems connected by API, and a EUR 10,000 payment still failed at clearing
explain:
Two banks connected their instant payment systems through an API.

The connection test passed. A message went out, a response came back.

Then a EUR 10,000 payment was accepted by the channel and rejected by clearing.

Here's how it happened:

→ Systems connected via API
→ Message sent, response received, connection declared working
→ EUR 10,000 payment accepted by the channel
→ Clearing rejects it, scheme rules do not match
→ Customer waits, both banks point at the connection that works

The assumption was:
"If the API connects, the payment works."

Why?

Connecting two instant payment systems through an API proves that a message can be sent and a response received, but it does not prove the payment will work end to end. The systems must also align on message formats, scheme rules, clearing, settlement, compliance and operations. Connectivity is the easiest part of the integration.

Connected is not interoperable.

BA Takeaway

An integration is not done when the API responds. It is done when a payment clears, settles, and reconciles under the scheme rules of both sides, with compliance and operations aligned.

Keep these controls separate:

→ API connectivity
→ Message formats
→ Scheme rules
→ Clearing and settlement
→ Compliance and operations

The real requirement isn't "Does the API respond?"

It's "What evidence proves a payment clears end to end?"

Have you seen an integration declared done on an API test alone?
takeaway: Connected is not interoperable.

title: A EUR 20,000 payment worked on UPI, then failed on FedNow for a reason no engineer could see
explain:
A bank connected to instant payment systems in several markets: UPI in India, SCT Inst in Europe, and FedNow and RTP in the United States.

A EUR 20,000 payment worked on one system.

The same payment failed on another, and the engineers found nothing wrong with the connection.

Here's how it happened:

→ Payment works on UPI in India
→ Same payment sent on FedNow in the US
→ Connection healthy, message well formed
→ Payment fails on scheme rules, not technology
→ Participants, operating hours and dispute processes differ by market

The assumption was:
"Instant payment systems are one system with different names."

Why?

UPI, SCT Inst, FedNow and RTP are not one system. The systems differ in scheme rules, participants, operating hours and dispute processes, so a payment that works in one market can fail in another for a non-technical reason. Technical connectivity and scheme alignment must both be designed.

Same payment, different rulebook.

BA Takeaway

When connecting to a new instant system, design the scheme alignment alongside the technical connection: rules, participants, hours, disputes. A healthy connection proves nothing about the scheme.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Technical connectivity
→ Scheme rules per market
→ Participants per market
→ Operating hours and dispute processes

The real requirement isn't "Is the connection up?"

It's "What evidence proves the payment fits this market's scheme?"

Have you seen a payment fail on a healthy connection because the scheme differed?
takeaway: Same payment, different rulebook.

title: One generic field set swallowed a EUR 30,000 payment's remittance data, and no one could reconcile it
explain:
A EUR 30,000 payment crossed two corridors, and each corridor sent slightly different fields.

The bank collapsed them into one generic field set.

The remittance data was lost, and the beneficiary could not reconcile the payment against the right invoice.

Here's how it happened:

→ Payment arrives with corridor A fields
→ Payment leaves with corridor B fields
→ Both sets collapsed into one generic set
→ Remittance data dropped in the collapse
→ Beneficiary cannot match the payment to an invoice

The assumption was:
"Similar fields are the same fields."

Why?

Different channels and corridors send similar but non-identical payment fields, and collapsing them into one generic set of fields loses information. A common data model must define how fields translate, how validation works, and what error semantics apply across different domestic rails. Without that model, small data differences become payment failures that are hard to trace.

Similar is not identical.

BA Takeaway

The common data model is the integration, not a document about it. Define the field translation, the validation, and the error meaning for every corridor before the first payment crosses.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Each corridor's fields, as sent
→ The field translation rules
→ Validation across rails
→ Error semantics, agreed

The real requirement isn't "Do the fields look the same?"

It's "What evidence proves no data is lost in translation?"

Have you seen a generic field set lose data a payment needed?
takeaway: Similar is not identical.

title: A father in India sent INR 50,000 to Singapore with just a mobile number, and the transfer failed on scope
explain:
A father in India sent INR 50,000 to a family member in Singapore using only the recipient mobile number.

The linkage between the two systems was live.

The transfer failed, because that account type was not covered by the linkage.

Here's how it happened:

→ Person in India sends INR 50,000 to Singapore
→ Sender uses only the recipient mobile number
→ Proxy identifier resolved to an account
→ Participating institution model routes the payment
→ Account type not covered by the linkage, payment rejected

The assumption was:
"If the linkage is live, every transfer works."

Why?

The linkage works through proxy identifiers and a participating institution model, where each side resolves the proxy to the right account. But the scope of the linkage must be validated, because not every account type or transaction type is covered. The first design question is always what the linkage actually covers.

Live does not mean everything is covered.

BA Takeaway

Before offering a linked payment, publish the scope: which account types, which transaction types, which direction. A linkage is defined by its limits as much as by its reach.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The proxy resolution
→ The participating institution model
→ The account types covered
→ The transaction types covered

The real requirement isn't "Is the linkage live?"

It's "What evidence proves this account and transaction type are in scope?"

Have you seen a linked payment fail because the scope was never checked?
takeaway: Live does not mean everything is covered.
